blocks.md:
Have you noticed native speakers starting sentences with *“…-는데”* before asking a question or making an offer?

- *“지금 마트에 가**는데**, 뭐 필요해요?”* (I am heading to the supermarket, do you need anything?)

For **all verbs in the present tense**, simply attach **-는데** directly to the stem regardless of batchim! *(Verbs ending in ㄹ drop the ㄹ: 살다 → 사는데)*

items.tip: I’m going to the supermarket now, do you need anything?
It’s raining outside, do you have an umbrella?
I’m eating lunch right now, want to join?

blocks.q: Attach the background connector -는데 to 마시다 (to drink):
blocks.why: All action verbs take -는데: 마시- + -는데 = 마시는데.

blocks.meaning: It is raining outside, do you have an umbrella?
blocks.why: 비가 오는데 sets the background before asking the question 우산 있어요?.

blocks.q: Put in order: "I'm going to the cafe right now, do you want to come along?"
I am going to the supermarket right now, do you need anything?
blocks.hint: 지금, 마트에 가다 → 가는데, 뭐 필요해요?

blocks.md:
While verbs take **-는데**, adjectives and nouns have slightly different endings:

1. **Adjectives** take **-(으)ㄴ데**:
- No batchim → **-ㄴ데** *(바쁘다 → 바쁜데, 예쁘다 → 예쁜데)*
- Has batchim → **-은데** *(좋다 → 좋은데, 작다 → 작은데)*
- **ㅂ irregular** → **-운데** *(춥다 → 추운데, 덥다 → 더운데)*

2. **Nouns** take **인데** *(학생인데, 일요일인데)*
3. **있다 / 없다** take **-는데** *(있는데, 없는데)*

items.tip: The weather is really nice today, shall we take a walk?
I’m a bit busy right now, let’s meet in 10 minutes.
Tomorrow is Sunday, what are you doing?

blocks.q: How do you attach the background connector to 덥다 (ㅂ irregular)?
blocks.why: 덥다 is a ㅂ irregular adjective! ㅂ changes to 우, so 덥- + -(으)ㄴ데 = 더운데.

blocks.meaning: The weather is really nice today, shall we go out?
blocks.why: 좋다 is an adjective with batchim, so it takes -은데: 좋은데.

blocks.hint: 덥다 is an adjective with ㅂ irregular: 덥다 → 더운데 (not 덥는데)!
blocks.why: Adjective 덥다 becomes 더운데: 오늘 날씨가 더운데 에어컨을 켜요.

blocks.q: The weather is really good today, shall we take a walk?
blocks.hint: 오늘 날씨가 정말 좋다 → 좋은데, 산책할까요?

blocks.md:
In Korean culture, direct refusals (*“I can’t go”*) can sound harsh. **-는데 / -(으)ㄴ데** is the native speaker’s magic key to softening their speech:

- *“가고 싶**은데**, 오늘은 약속이 있어요.”* (I want to go, but I have plans today.)

It cushions the refusal and gives context before stating the conflict.

items.tip: I want to go, but I have plans today.
I want to eat lunch, do you want to go together?
I have plenty of time, but no money.

blocks.q: Which sentence sounds the most polite and natural for declining an invitation?
blocks.why: -는데 softens the refusal by explaining your feeling before the obstacle.

blocks.meaning: I want to have lunch, do you want to go together?
blocks.why: -고 싶다 is an adjective form, so it takes -은데: 싶- + -은데 = 싶은데.

blocks.q: Build: "I want to buy clothes, where should I go?"
I want to have lunch, do you want to go together?
blocks.hint: 점심을 먹고 싶다 → 먹고 싶은데, 같이 갈래요?

title.ko: 4강. 실전 대화: 거절과 부탁을 부드럽게 넘기기
title.en: Lesson 4. Real-Life Conversation: Softening Refusals and Requests

blocks.h: Using Background Endings to Soften Refusals and Requests
blocks.md:
In Korean culture, direct blunt answers like **안 돼요** (No) or **못 가요** (I can't go) can sound abrupt or harsh.

Instead, Koreans soften their speech by setting up a background clause with **-는데 / -(으)ㄴ데**:

- **Polite Refusal:** 제가 지금 일이 좀 **많은데요**… (I have quite a bit of work right now, so…)
- **Softening an Invitation / Request:** 오늘 저녁에 시간 **있는데**, 같이 밥 먹을래요? (I have some free time this evening, would you like to eat together?)
- **Leading into a Question:** 사진을 찍고 **싶은데**, 여기서 찍어도 돼요? (I’d like to take a photo, is it okay to take one here?)

head: Goal
Direct & Blunt (Avoid)
Polite & Soft (-는데 / -(으)ㄴ데)
rows: 약속이 있어서 못 갈 것 같은데요…

blocks.md: Ending a sentence with **-는데요 / -(으)ㄴ데요** leaves the ending open and gentle. It softens the mood and lets the listener read between the lines without any harshness!

items.ch: 오늘 저녁에 같이 식사할 수 있어요? — 죄송해요, 오늘은 선약이 있는데요.
items.tip: Can you have dinner together tonight? — Sorry, I have a prior engagement… (-ㄴ데요 soft refusal)
I am looking for the way, where is the subway station? (-는데 leading into question)

items.ch: 이 옷 정말 예쁜데, 한번 입어 봐도 돼요?
items.tip: This outfit is really pretty, may I try it on? (-ㄴ데 setting context)

blocks.q: A coworker invites you to coffee, but you are very busy right now. Which response is the most polite and natural?
blocks.why: Ending with -ㄴ데요 softens the refusal gently: 바쁘다 + -ㄴ데요 → **바쁜데요…**.

blocks.q: How do you conjugate ‘있다’ (to have/exist) into this background-setting form?
blocks.why: Words with 있다 / 없다 always attach -는데: 있 + 는데 → **있는데**.

blocks.q: Match each verb/adjective type with its correct background ending.

blocks.meaning: I'd like to go to the subway station, which way should I go?
blocks.why: 싶다 is an adjective (with 받침 ㅂ), so it takes -은데: 싶 + 은데 → **싶은데**.

blocks.q: Conjugate 멀다 (to be far, ㄹ adjective) with -(으)ㄴ데: 「거기는 조금 ___ 지하철을 탈까요?」
blocks.why: For ㄹ adjectives, ㄹ drops and attaches ㄴ데: 멀다 → **먼데**.

blocks.say: 죄송한데, 사진 한 장만 찍어 주실 수 있나요?
blocks.rom: joe-song-han-de, sa-jin han jang-man jjig-eo ju-sil su iss-na-yo
blocks.q: Say it aloud politely asking someone to take a photo.
